en: Śrī is the discourse on the body;
he is a skilled six-legged bee whose mind resembles a vessel filled with the fragrance of the lotus feet of Śrīkānta’s beloved.
Having paid homage to the venerable Śrī Lakṣmaṇārya, the infinite Sudhī composes this discourse on the body, which is consistent with the essential meaning.
"First, the ground for the application of the word 'body' (śarīra) is here examined.

For "bodiness" (śarīratva), which constitutes the ground for the application of the term 'body', is certainly not a universal (jāti), because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to establish it.

Nor should it be argued that the recurring cognition "this is a body, this is a body" alone establishes [the existence of the universal], because an recurring cognition establishes a universal only when there is no sublation; for in our system (siddhānta), since such a recurring cognition has as its object the configuration (saṃsthāna), it is impossible for it to establish a universal distinct from that.

Nor should it be argued: "Since configuration (*saṃsthāna*) consists of the conjunction of parts and so forth, it differs with each individual instance; how then can it be the object of a uniform cognition? For in the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others, just as the universal "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), which is distinct due to the differences between gold, silver, copper, clay, and other pots, is nonetheless the object of the uniform cognition "this is a pot, this is a pot," so too is the case for configuration. Furthermore, if "pot-ness" were one and the same across pots made of gold, silver, and so on, the logical fault of "overlapping" (*sāṅkarya*) would result.

Furthermore—the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) intended as the nature of universals such as "cowness" is not, in fact, of the nature of a conjunction of parts; for if it were, then since such a configuration is absent in qualities like color and taste, as well as in substances such as the self (*ātman*), one would be forced to postulate a separate universal for those cases as well. Rather, it is simply the cognition whose object consists of all individual cows, related to them through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*).

And that very [universal] appears as the qualifier by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) in cognitions such as "this is a cow"; thus, there is no difference in the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) due to the difference in individual instances. Furthermore, it is precisely that which is the object of cognitions regarding jars and so forth—namely, that which is inclusive across all jar-individuals and non-overextended—that is the universal *ghaṭatva* (jar-ness) and so on; it is this very thing that is the delimitor of the effect-nature produced by the staff and other causes, and the delimitor of the denotability of the word "jar"—as is clear in another treatise.
Having this in mind, it was stated in the *Jijñāsādhikaraṇa-bhāṣya*:
"That which is called configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is the specific form unique to each thing; therefore, one should contemplate the configuration according to the actual state of the object."
And it is said in the *Nyāyasiddhāñjana*:

"The linguistic usage of 'belonging to a single class' is established through specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as there is a usage of unity in reference to a heap, an army, an assembly, and so forth. And this limiting adjunct is the simultaneous presence [in memory] of many things within a single recollection."

And thus—according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), a universal (*jāti*) is simply the cognition having that many objects as its content, and it is accepted that such a cognition manifests by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*). Therefore, in the present case as well, if one accepts that the cognitions "this is a body," "this is a body," and so forth, have as their object the universal consisting of the cognition having those [bodies] as its content, and if one further accepts that this very [universal] is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "body," then the word "body" would incur the impossibility of being a relative term (*sasambandhika*), like the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*). For being a relative term consists in the capacity to arouse an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding a related entity.

And that [definition] is not tenable if it were based solely on birth as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), as is the case with words such as "cow" and the like. Therefore, intending to state that a ground for application distinct from that must be asserted, it was said in the *Śrībhāṣya* regarding the passage "but not because of the existence of an example":

"The definition of a body (*śarīra*) must be accepted as follows: whatever substance is capable of being entirely controlled and sustained by a conscious being for its own sake, and whose very nature consists solely in being subordinate to that being—that is its body."
"In this regard, those who follow the *Śrutaprakāśikā* [state] the first definition:

'The body of a conscious being is that substance which can be controlled by that being in its entirety for its own purposes. The meaning is that the ground for the application of the term 'body' (*śarīra*) is the state of being 'governed' (*niyāmyatva*), which consists in being the locus of all one's own activities prompted by the activity [of another], as seen in cases such as 'the servant is governed by the king,' where it is understood that the servant is the locus of activities prompted by the king's volition (*kṛti*). In expressions such as 'this is the body of this living being (*jīva*),' the meaning of the genitive case is the property of being contained (*ādheyatva*)."

Because there is a positive concomitance (anvaya) with respect to that which constitutes a portion of the category of "body" (śarīra-padārtha), the cognition arises: "This is that which possesses a general bodily movement (ceṣṭā-sāmānya) prompted by an effort (kṛti) residing in this living being. And in the same manner as stated, the cognition in such passages as "He whose self is the body," or "He whose earth is the body," should be inferred. Here, the inclusion of the word "general" (sāmānya) is for the purpose of avoiding the conventional usage "the servant is the king's body"; for although a specific movement residing in the servant is prompted by the king's effort, the general class of movement lacks that prompting.

And thus, even in the case of another's body, vital breaths, sense organs, and so forth, they do not constitute objects of the conventional designation "body" with respect to that [other] soul; because the general movement occurring in another's body is not caused by the volition of that [specific] soul, and because the vital breaths and sense organs persist until the dissolution of the universe even after the liberation of this [present] soul, the general movement of those [organs] is not caused by the volition of that [liberated soul].

If it is accepted that the knowledge constituting the self (dharmabhūtajñāna) possesses the commonality of being an activity prompted by the effort of the living being (jīvakṛti), then—in order to preclude such conventional designations as "knowledge is its body" and so forth—the property of being the counter-positive of a relation whose relatum-ness (anuyogitā) is delimited by knowledge must also be included in the aforementioned definition. Furthermore, a relation having knowledge as its counter-positive does not have a relatum-ness delimited by knowledge.

Thus, the result is that the basis for the application of the term "body" (śarīra) is the state of being related to a general volitional effort induced by an action, while having as its relatum a relation whose locus is delimited by consciousness.

In expressions such as "this is the body of the soul" (*etajjīvasya idaṃ śarīram*), one should infer the understanding by accepting that the sense of the genitive case—namely, the state of being located (*ādheyatva*)—is construed with the relatum (*anuyogitā*) which is a part of the referent of the word "body," and with the action (*kṛti*). Since a subtle, specific kind of movement induced by the respective actions of the Lord is admitted to exist in living bodies, as well as in trees and so forth, and in mountains and so forth which are the bodies of the Lord, there is no inconsistency in their being objects of the conventional usage of the term "body."
And it is said in the *Nyāyasiddhāñjana*: "Because the extremely subtle specific regulation [of the soul] within stationary beings and the like is difficult for people such as ourselves to perceive."

If it is argued that the aforementioned definition is under-extended (*avyāpti*) because there is no evidence for the existence of specific movement in immobile things such as mountains due to their subtlety, then, out of dissatisfaction with this very point, another definition is stated in the *Śrībhāṣya*:
"The body of a conscious being is that substance which can be supported by that being in its entirety."

The meaning is that the basis for the application of the term "body" (*śarīra*) is the state of possessing a conjunction in general that prevents one's own falling, where the falling has as its counter-positive the action (effort) initiated by [that agent]. In expressions such as "this is the body of this soul," the sense of the genitive case—namely, "locatedness" (*ādheyatva*)—is construed with the action; thus, the cognition is: "this [body] possesses a conjunction in general that prevents its own falling, where the falling has as its counter-positive the action initiated by that [soul] residing in this [soul]. Here, by the inclusion of the word "general" (*sāmānya*), there is no undesirable consequence of the usage "my son is the body of his father."

For although the specific conjunction that prevents the father's downfall—which has the son as its counter-correlative—is produced by the father's ritual act, the general category of such conjunctions is not produced by it.

Nor should it be argued that even so, it is difficult to avoid the consequence that the designation "body" would apply to such lice and so forth as are produced on someone's head and perish right there; for the conjunction of which the counter-positive is the body of the louse has the soul of that [louse] as its relatum (anuyogin), and also the head of this [person] as its relatum.

In this regard, although the conjunction having this head as its locus (*anuyogin*) and the body of a louse or similar creature as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is prompted by this [person's] effort, there is no occurrence of the aforementioned fault because the conjunction having that [louse's] soul as its locus is not prompted by this effort. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the conventional usage "this is Caitra’s body" would be untenable; for although the conjunction having this body as its counter-correlate and the self as its locus is prompted by Caitra’s effort, the conjunction having the ground as its locus is not prompted by Caitra’s effort.

Furthermore, since even the conjunction with the ground is produced by the action of Caitra’s body, it does not lose its status as being prompted by Caitra’s effort (*kṛti*). If the condition of "having itself as the counter-correlator" (*svapratiyogikatva*) were not included [in the definition], the expression "this is Caitra’s body" would be untenable; for in a conjunction that has the ground as its correlate and a cloth as its counter-correlator—which occurs even without an action of the body—there is an absence of being prompted by Caitra’s effort. Therefore, that [condition] must be included.

"Now, [it may be argued: since falling is necessarily applicable to substances possessing gravity (*gurutva*), even if one accepts that a conjunction having such a substance as its counter-correlative acts as an obstacle to falling, a conjunction having a soul (*jīva*)—which is devoid of gravity—as its counter-correlative cannot possibly act as an obstacle to falling. Consequently, scriptural usages such as 'He whose self is the body' would be untenable. If this is said, we reply: No. Precisely by the force of scriptures indicating that [the Lord] is the substratum of the universe and so forth, a conjunction having the Lord as its correlate and the soul and so forth as its counter-correlative [is established]."

This is because [the status of being a substratum] is admitted to be the prevention of falling, since the nature of being a substratum (*ādhāratā*) consists in being the relatum (*anuyogitva*) of a conjunction that prevents falling. Furthermore, even if one were to abandon the property of preventing falling and instead accept as the basis for the application of the term "body" (*śarīra*) the general property of a conjunction whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is prompted by volition (*kṛti*), there would still be no deficiency in the position.

Regarding the multiple bodies assumed at once by yogins such as Saubhari, and those multiple bodies of the liberated one established by such scriptural texts as "He becomes singlefold; he becomes twofold," there is no fault; for although there is an absence of the relation of subject and object (anuyogi-pratiyogitva) between the individual soul and all those bodies, the fact that the general conjunction having those bodies as its counter-correlates (pratiyogika-saṃyoga-sāmānya) is invariably caused by the respective selves and their respective modes remains intact.

In this regard, the definition of a body as explained in the *Nirukta* suffers from the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) with respect to all-pervading substances such as time (*kāla*), and so forth. This is because, according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), an eternal mutual conjunction between all-pervading entities is accepted; consequently, it is impossible for the general category of conjunction having time and the like as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to be produced by the activity (*kṛti*) of the Lord (*Īśvara*). Furthermore, if the basis for the application of the term "body" (*śarīra*) were defined as "having a general conjunction produced by one's own activity as its counter-correlate," then the property of being "produced" (*janyatva*) would be subject to the dilemma of whether it consists in being the counter-correlate of a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) or the counter-correlate of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), and so on. This would result in a plurality of meanings for the word "body" due to the resulting difference in the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
Therefore, another definition has been stated:
"The body of a conscious being is that substance which, in its entirety and without remainder, possesses a single nature identical to that being."

For being a "subsidiary" (śeṣatva) consists in conferring an excellence upon that [primary entity]. In the present context, the excellence residing in that [entity] takes the form of either effect-ness or cause-ness. And the conferring of that [excellence] consists in being its delimiting factor (avacchedakatva).

Thus, the meaning is: the basis for the application of the term "body" (śarīra) is the state of being the delimiting factor of either effect-ness or cause-ness, where such [effect-ness or cause-ness] is delimited by a cognition and related to it through the relation of non-separability (apṛthaksiddhi) as its substratum (anuyogitā).

Since Brahman qualified by the subtle sentient and insentient is the cause, and that same [Brahman] qualified by the gross sentient and insentient is the effect, the status of being the body of the world is established because the property of being a delimiting adjunct (avacchedakatva) of either effect-hood or cause-hood residing in Brahman exists in the entire phenomenal universe (prapañca). Thus, there is the justification for such scriptural usage as: "He whose self is the body," "He whose earth is the body," and "The entire world is Your body."

In that context, since the sense of the genitive—the state of being the locus (*ādheyatva*)—is construed with either the effect-ness or the cause-ness [of the object], there arises the cognition: "Earth, etc., is that which delimits either the cause-ness or the effect-ness residing in Brahman. Since even the individual soul (*jīva*) brings about effects such as pleasure and pain only when qualified by a body, that body serves as the delimiter of the soul's cause-ness; thus, the conventional usage "this is the body of this soul" is logically sustained.

"Even though"—the soul's causality with respect to effects such as pleasure does not consist in its being qualified by the body; for, since there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanā*) to determine whether the causality lies in the self as qualified by the body or the body as qualified by the self, this would result in the undesirable consequence of two distinct and cumbersome causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Rather, according to the analogy of the staff and the wheel, there are two separate causalities belonging to the body and the self respectively. Consequently, [statements] such as "this is the body of this soul" would not be tenable.

"Nevertheless"—even though the body and the self are each individually causes when causehood is introduced in its general form as "being a motivator" (*prayojakatā*) as defined above, there is no impairment to their being the motivators for the production of the effect by virtue of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of one qualified by the other; thus, the aforementioned linguistic usage is established precisely by taking the delimitation of the motivatorhood residing in the living being (*jīva*).

Furthermore, by incorporating the qualification of being "delimited by the relation of non-separate existence" (*apṛthaksiddha-sambandha*) within the aforementioned deliminatorship (*avacchedakatā*), there is no unwanted consequence of the linguistic usage "the servant is the body of the king," even though the king (qualified by the servant) performs an action. This is because, although the servant acts as a deliminator of the king's status as a producer of an effect through the relation of master and servant (*svasvāmibhāva*), he lacks the status of being a deliminator delimited by the relation of non-separate existence. Additionally, the inclusion of the property of having a "locus-ness delimited by cognition" (*jñānāvacchinnānuyogitākatva*) is for the purpose of precluding the linguistic usage "cognition is his body."

By this—namely, by the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*) whereby the body qualified by the soul (*jīva-viśiṣṭa-śarīra*) would also be a causal factor for the production of an effect—the following objection is refuted: that it would follow from usage that the soul is the body of the body, because the soul serves as the delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) of the body’s status as a producer of effects through the relation of non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddhi*). [The author replies: Even though the soul is the delimiting adjunct of the body’s status as a producer of effects through the relation of being located (*ādheyatā*), which consists in being the counter-correlative of the relation of non-separate existence whose own relatum (*anuyogin*) is the soul; [The sentence continues: ...[the objection remains refuted]. (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly, but the logical structure indicates the conclusion of the argument.)

This is because [the soul] does not possess such a status through the relation of inseparable inherence (*apṛthaksiddhi*) where the relatumhood (*anuyogitā*) is delimited by knowledge. Furthermore, since even liberated beings (*mukta*) produce effects such as movement only by being qualified by a body, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) with respect to their bodies and so forth.
The fourth definition, which is the fruition of these three characteristics, is set forth in the *Nyāyasiddhāñjana*:
"That substance which is an inseparably established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) of a conscious being in whatever state it may be, that is its body."

The meaning is that the ground for the application of the term "body" (*śarīra*) is the state of being a counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) residing in the same locus as substantiality (*dravyatva*), as determined by a relation of non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddhi*) whose relatum is delimited by knowledge (*jñāna*). In expressions such as "this is the body of this living being," the referent of the word "body" is that which is delimited by a counter-positivity residing in the same locus as substantiality, as determined by a relation of non-separate existence whose relatum is delimited by knowledge.

Since the meaning of the word ending in the genitive case—the state of residing in this living being—is construed with the relatum (anuyogitā) as delimited by the knowledge of that one part, the resulting cognition is: "This [body] is delimited by a counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva) which co-occurs with substantiality (dravyatva) as defined by a relation of non-separate existence (apṛthaksiddhi), wherein the relatum is delimited by knowledge residing in this living being. This is because, according to the established doctrine (siddhānta), since attributive knowledge (dharmabhūtajñāna) is a substance, there exists a relation of non-separate existence between knowledge and the self, just as there is between the body and the self.

The inclusion of the property of having an anuyogitā (the relation of being the locus) delimited by knowledge is for the purpose of excluding the linguistic usage "knowledge is its body," because such a counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) coexists with the category of substance (dravyatva). Furthermore, since the counter-correlativity of the relation of inseparable inherence (apṛthaksiddhi), which has an anuyogitā delimited by knowledge, exists in the dimension (parimāṇa) residing in the self, the inclusion of coexistence with the category of substance within that counter-correlativity is for the purpose of excluding the linguistic usage "dimension is its body."

Nor should it be argued that this definition lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of Saubhari’s bodies and the like, on the grounds that while the quality of non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddhatva*) from the individual soul (*jīva*) exists in one body, it is impossible in another body. For the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "body" is simply the state of being a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) residing in the same locus as substance-ness (*dravyatva*), as defined by non-separate existence.

In expressions such as "this is the body of this soul" (*etaj-jīvasyedam śarīram*), the meaning of the genitive case is understood as either (1) having a locus-hood delimited by a cognition residing in itself, or (2) being the locus of its own cognition; it is through one of these two relations that the qualified meaning is obtained. Even in the case of the bodies of Saubhari and others—which are not in a state of non-separation (*apṛthaksiddhi*) from the soul—the relation of non-separation from cognition is established by the maxim "like a lamp, there is an entry [of the soul]" (*pradīpavad āveśaḥ*). Thus, by taking the property of being the counter-correlative of a relation of non-separation whose locus is its own cognition, the linguistic usage of "body" is maintained even in those cases.

If it is objected: "The relation of non-separable establishment (*apṛthaksiddhi*) between the body and the self is not possible, because the relation of non-separable establishment is accepted only for those things that are incapable of existing without being related as long as they exist; for we observe that a dead body continues to exist even while devoid of connection with the living soul, which shows that the two are not incapable of existing without being related as long as they exist," we say no. For there is no inconsistency, since it is accepted that a substance which previously existed as a body perishes at the very moment immediately following its separation from consciousness.

And likewise, in the *Śrībhāṣya* on the passage "But not because of the existence of an example," it says: "A dead body, however, begins to disintegrate at the very moment of separation from consciousness and is fully dissolved in the next moment. The conventional usage of the term 'body' applies to it only because it is a portion of the aggregate that was previously designated as a body."
"In the same way, the avoidance of under-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding the previous definitions should also be inferred," so they say.

"But others [hold that]": the commentary beginning with "of which sentient being... (*yasya cetanasya*) refers only to a single definition, and not to three definitions. This is because there is an absence of words such as "and so forth" (*ādi*) or "or" (*vā*) that would indicate [multiple definitions]; furthermore, it contradicts the commentary which states that "the grounds for the application [of the term] (*pravṛttinimitta*) are the states of being supported (*ādheyatva*), being commanded (*vidheyatva*), and being subordinate (*śeṣatva*). In that case, although there is no over-extension (*atiprasakti*) when each individual property is taken as the delimiting factor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), the acceptance of the collection [of all three] as such is due solely to the experienced cognition of the states of being supported, being commanded, and being subordinate from the word "body" (*śarīra*).

Furthermore, after the cognition produced by the sentence "this body belongs to this soul," no one ever experiences a doubt regarding the soul's being the locus (*ādheyatva*) and so forth, with respect to the specific object denoted by "this" (*idam-dārtha*). In this context, since it is necessary for the triad of properties beginning with "being the locus" to be the objects of the cognition produced by the word "body" (*śarīra*), it is essential that the collective whole [of these three] serves as the delimitor of the word's denotative power (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). This is just as, although "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*) is not over-extensive, the property of "being the agent of production from mud" (*paṅkajanikartṛtva*) is accepted as the delimitor of the denotative power of words such as "paṅkaja" (lotus) in order to account for the resulting cognition.

Now, [one might object]: even though the triad consisting of being the substratum (ādheyatva) and so forth is understood from the sentence "this body belongs to this soul," it is not necessary for that triad to be the delimitor of the denotative capacity (śakyatāvacchedaka). For even if only the state of being the substratum (ādheyatva) serves as the delimitor of the denotative capacity, the states of being the thing enjoined (vidheyatva) and being subordinate (śeṣatva) can still be manifested through the force of presumptive implication (arthāpatti).

If it is argued: "In our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since it is accepted that not only the object of the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) produced by words, but also the object of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), appears in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there is a possibility here of a presumption (*arthāpatti*) such as: 'Corporeality (*śarīratva*) is inexplicable without being something located (*ādheyatva*) and subordinate (*śeṣatva*). For this very reason, in cases such as 'Bring water with a jar,' the appearance in verbal cognition of 'not having a hole'—which is the object of a presumption based on the fact that fetching water is inexplicable without not having a hole—is indeed an empirical fact. [Response: This is not so.

They say: "Because, in accordance with the Bhāṣya—'Since that which is obtained through implication (ākṣepataḥ) must be understood as being precisely that which is denotative (ābhidhānika)'—the appearance of the object of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) in verbal cognition is accepted only in cases where the capacity [of words] is impossible."

Since it is stated in the *Śrutaprakāśikā* that in passages such as "He whose body is the Vedas" and "He whose body is the sacrifices," the words "Veda" and "sacrifice" refer to the presiding deities (*abhimānidevatā*) thereof, there is no deficiency even if the aforementioned definition of a body does not apply to the Vedas and sacrifices themselves.

Even though it is possible for the referent "body" (śarīra) to enter into a relation of non-difference with the substance that constitutes one part of the ritual act of sacrifice—which consists of the relinquishment of a substance intended for a deity—and since it is also possible for it to enter into a relation with the "knowledge" that forms part of the etymological meaning of the word *veda*—derived from the analysis "they cause to know" (*vedayanti*) as a means of knowledge—the assumption of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the words *veda* and *yajña* would be redundant.

Nevertheless, in order to avoid such linguistic usages as "motion is a quality" (gamanaṃ guṇaḥ) by intending an identity-connection (*abheda-sambandha*) with the quality [of conjunction]—which is a single part of the referent of the word "motion" (the category of action consisting of a movement conducive to conjunction)—it is necessary that the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by a word be a cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) through the relation of primary qualificandumness (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*). With this in mind, and recognizing that even in the present case an identity-connection with a single part [of the referent] is impossible, [the author states the following].

There is no inconsistency because the use of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is accepted for the two words *veda* and *yajña*. It should be noted that Gadādhara and others have demonstrated the cognition of identity—where the meaning of the word *parama* (supreme) is construed with beauty (*saundarya*), which is one part of the meaning of the word *sundara* (beautiful), and with knowledge (*jñāna*), which is one part of the meaning of the word *ātman* (self)—in such expressions as "the Supreme Self is supremely beautiful," precisely because there is no other possible way to account for it; for without such a construction, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) could not be established.

The logicians (*tārkikāḥ*), however, following the sūtra "The body is the substratum of movement, sense organs, and objects," hold that the ground for the application of the term "body" (*śarīra*) is either: (1) possessing movement while being a final composite (*antyāvayavin*); (2) being the substratum of the sense organs while being a final composite; or (3) being the delimiting factor of experience (*bhoga*) while being a final composite. In that regard, in the first case—such as in the expression "this is the body of this living being"—the understanding is that the meaning of the genitive case, namely "being produced by volitional effort" (*kṛti-prayojyatva*), is related to "possessing movement," which is a part of the referent of the word "body. Thus, the cognition is: "that which possesses movement [and is a final composite] is produced by the volitional effort of this living being."

"In the second [interpretation]," because the meaning of the genitive case—namely, the status of being a generator of cognition—is construed with the sense-organ (*indriya*), which is one part of the referent of the word "body," the resulting cognition is: "This is that which is the locus of a sense-organ residing in this living being, which generates cognition and is co-located with the state of being a final constituent (*antyāvayavitva*). "In the third [interpretation]," the resulting cognition is: "This is that which possesses a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā*) co-located with the state of being a final constituent, [and] which is the locus of the meaning of the genitive case, namely, the property of being contained (*ādheyatva*). They say that the phrase "in all cases, the 'satisfying the condition' (*satyantam')" is included in order to exclude such conventional usage as "The hand is the body of this [person]."

That [definition] is to be considered: if, in the first alternative (*prathamakalpa*), by the word "volitional movement" (*ceṣṭā*) one intends to express action in general, then the undesirable consequence would follow that a pot (*ghaṭa*) is the body of Devadatta; for the state of possessing an action produced by Devadatta’s volition—which is co-extensive with being a final whole (*antyāvayavitva*)—exists in the pot. If, however, by the word "volitional movement" one intends a specific kind of action conducive to the attainment of the beneficial or the avoidance of the harmful, or an action of a distinct class (*vijātīya*), then there arises the undesirable consequence that Devadatta is the body of God (*īśvara*), a usage not accepted by you.

Because the property of possessing activity prompted by the action of God exists in Devadatta; and even if the aforementioned over-extension is avoided by accepting that the meaning of the genitive case is "having an uncommon cause in the form of an action," the under-extension of the stated definition to stones and the like—which constitute the bodies of Ahalyā and others—is unavoidable. In the second [alternative], if one intends to mean "possessing sense organs" by way of inherence (*samavāya*), there is the fault of impossibility [since the self does not possess organs in that manner] and over-extension to the parts of the sense organs.

If that [the body] is intended by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), there is the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to jars and the like; and if it is intended by way of the relation of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the cognition produced by itself, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of the bodies of Rāma and others, because God’s cognition is eternal and, as being all-pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), is independent of a delimiting factor; furthermore, there is non-pervasion in the case of the bodies of Ahalyā and others, which consist of stone, wood, and so forth. In the third [definition], there is over-extension to houses and the like.

In cases such as "the lion's roar in the forest," just as the forest serves as the delimiting locus (*avacchedaka*) for the sound produced within the confines of the lion's throat, so too can a house or similar location serve as the delimiting locus for an experience produced within the confines of the body; this is also supported by the common linguistic usage, "his enjoyment [occurs] in the house."

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the definition of "not being delimited by a location distinct from its own parts" is included within the delimitation as defined by experience (*bhoga*); for the house is a delimiting factor only when it is itself delimited by the body, and since this [qualification] is a further specification of "location," there is no impossibility; and even though the delimitation residing in the body is delimited by its own parts (in accordance with the experience "pleasure in the foot"), it is nonetheless not delimited by a location distinct from those parts. This cannot be maintained, because it would result in the body of another person having the status of a "body" for one who has entered it.

Furthermore, because the experience of the Lord is an all-pervasive occurrence (*vyāpyavṛtti*), there is no established delimitor (*avacchedaka*) for it; consequently, the definition would fail to apply (*avyāpti*) to such things as the body of Rāma.

And likewise, regarding the [Brahma-sūtra] statement, "Moreover, it is untenable because of the consequence that [the individual soul] would be like that [the Supreme Self] at the time of dissolution," the Śrībhāṣya states:

"Nor is 'being a body' (śarīratva) simply 'being an abode of experience,' for the status of being a body is not established in the case of houses and other such things which serve as abodes of experience. If it is argued that 'an abode of experience is precisely that wherein one who is already present experiences pleasure and pain,' we say no; for the body of another person—which serves as the abode of experience for the pleasure and pain produced by entering another's body—is not established as being the 'body' of the one who has entered."

"But for Īśvara, who is by his very nature eternally established in unsurpassed bliss, it is impossible that there should be a rule regarding the two categories of conscious and unconscious entities serving as the locus for his enjoyment. Thus [it is said].

He raises the objection regarding the nature of being a locus (*āyatanatva*) as being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) with the words: "wherein [the experience] of that which is present... The meaning is that, by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of pleasure and so forth belongs to that which has an unconditioned delimitation residing in that very thing wherein the experience of pleasure or pain occurs for one who is present. This is because the sense of the particle *eva* (only) in the phrase "wherein... only" is construed with the delimitation denoted by the suffix *-tra*, such that it signifies "not delimited by any location other than its own parts. Thus, the purport of the Commentary lies precisely in the objection we have stated, beginning with "but not... (*na ca*).

It should be understood that bliss possesses both unsurpassedness (*niratiśayatva*) and all-pervasive existence (*vyāpyavṛttitva*). Therefore, the definition stated in the *Śrībhāṣya* alone is consistent with usage in both worldly and Vedic contexts. Consequently, since insentient entities as well as sentient entities are the body of the Supreme Self, and since words denoting a body refer ultimately to the embodied one, the use of grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇa*) in such passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman," "This Self is Brahman," and "That thou art" is logically established.

For this very reason, the statement—"Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms"—is logically consistent as the evolution of names and forms preceded by entry on the part of the Supreme Self (paramātman). In the phrase "by means of this living self," the meaning is "by me, having the living being as my body.

Otherwise, if one were to accept that the individual soul (jīvātman) alone is the agent of entry in accordance with the literal reading, there would arise a contradiction with other scriptural passages establishing the Supreme Self as the agent of entry, such as: "He entered that very [being]; having entered it, He became the formed and the formless."

"But if this is so"—then the use of the instrumental case (*ātmanā*) is untenable, because the agent is already expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in the word *vyākaravāṇi* ("I shall manifest"), according to the rule that the instrumental is prescribed only when the agent is not already expressed (*anabhihite kartari*). For the meaning of the grammatical injunction regarding the instrumental case and so forth is as follows: the instrumental and other such cases occur after that which is itself [the base] and lacks the intention to convey the agency (and so on) residing in a word generally co-occurring with it and distinct from its own subsequent suffix. Here, "itself" (*sva*) refers to the base of the instrumental case and so forth.

In examples such as "caitreṇa pacyate taṇḍulaḥ" (the rice is cooked by Caitra), the word *svam* refers to the word "Caitra. Since there exists an absence of the intention to convey agency with respect to the general class of words other than the suffix following that [word] which is co-occurrent with it, the use of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is justified. However, in the present case, such a *svam* is not the word "self" (*ātman*), because within the general class of words including the *tiṅ*-suffixes that are co-occurrent with and follow it, there is indeed the presence of the intention to convey agency.

And it is not the case that, although the intentionality of being the agent of the act of explaining (*vyākaraṇa*) exists in *tiṅ*-suffixes and the like, the absence of the intentionality of being the agent of the act of entering (*anupraveśa*) exists in all words co-occurring with itself—excluding the subsequent suffix following it—and therefore the third case ending is justified after the word *ātman*.

It should not be argued that [the rule] means: "The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth occur after a word that possesses a general status as a word distinct from its own co-occurring subsequent suffix, provided that it lacks the intentionality of denoting agency (*kartṛtva*) as determined by any action whatsoever co-occurring with itself, which is grounded in the object that constitutes its own primary intended meaning. For if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a third case ending occurring after the word *caitra* in such examples as "Caitra eats cooked food" (*pakvāni bhuṅkte caitraḥ*).

The word *svaṃ* [in the rule] refers to the word *caitra*, because it possesses the general property of being co-occurrent with other words (such as *pacati*) while lacking the intentionality (*tātparya*) directed toward any particular agenthood of cooking that resides in the object (the meaning) intended by that [word *caitra*]. Therefore, the meaning of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) must be stated as follows: "The third case ending (*tṛtīyādi*) occurs after that *svaṃ* which possesses the general property of being co-occurrent with other words and lacks the intentionality directed toward the agenthood as defined by the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*) residing in the object intended by that *svaṃ*."

In expressions such as "Caitra eats cooked [food]," there is no inconsistency, because the property of having as its intended meaning the agency in the primary action—which resides in Caitra and consists of being the agent of eating—is indeed present in the *tiṅ* suffix and other elements included within the general category of words co-occurring with that [noun].

"If it is argued: 'In the present context, since the status of being the primary agent of the act of grammatical derivation (vyākaraṇa)—which resides in the meaning that is the intended referent of the word *ātman*—is indeed present in the *tiṅ*-suffixes and so forth included within the general category of words co-occurring with [the word *ātman*], such a [co-occurring] word itself cannot be the word *ātman*; therefore, the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is unjustified'—to this we reply:

In the view of the Naiyāyikas and others who do not accept a difference in objective relations (*viṣayatā*) among cognitions of the same form, there would be an inconsistency regarding the use of the accusative case in sentences such as 'Maitra sees the pot being seen by Caitra.'"

The objecthood (*karmatva*), which consists in being an object as defined by both the act of seeing Caitra and the act of seeing Maitra, is one and the same. Since the *kṛt* suffix [in *dṛṣṭa*] possesses the intended meaning of that agency (*kartṛtva*) residing in the jar—which consists in being an object as defined by the primary action and so forth—among the general set of words co-occurring with it, such a word as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is not itself [the word expressing that agency]. Therefore, the meaning of rules such as "anabhihite kartari" (Pāṇini 2.3.1) is simply this: when the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is not intended to be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of agency and so forth, the third case suffix (*tṛtīyā*) is employed.

The meaning is that when the agency (*kartṛtva*) is not intended to be expressed as a qualifier of the nominal stem's meaning (*prātipadikārtha*), [the nominative applies]. Conversely, by emphasizing the restrictive sense, when the agency is intended to be expressed as the qualificand of the nominal stem's meaning, the conclusion must be accepted that the third case suffix (*tṛtīyā*) follows.

In examples such as "Maitra sees the pot being seen by Caitra," the accusative (*dvitīyā*) is justified because the objecthood (*karmatva*) is intended to be expressed as the qualificand of the nominal stem's meaning. Likewise, in examples such as "having entered by means of this living self" (*anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya*), the third case is justified because the agency is intended to be expressed as the qualificand of the nominal stem's meaning.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the usage "Caitra cooks with [the instrument] Caitra" (*caitreṇa pacati*), based on the intention to express cooking qualified by the agency of Caitra and others. Likewise, in a situation where the cooking has both Caitra and Maitra as its agents, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "Maitra cooks with Caitra" (*caitreṇa pacati maitraḥ*), based on the intention to convey the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) that "Maitra is the agent of the cooking whose agent is Caitra."

If it is argued that, by accepting the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that the agenthood expressed by the third case suffix (*tṛtīyārtha-kartṛtva*) is construed with an action that has not itself become a qualifier of another agenthood, one can avoid the aforementioned undesirable consequence; yet, in cases such as *caitreṇa pācayati maitraḥ* ("Caitra causes Maitra to cook"), there would still be the impossibility of construing the agenthood denoted by the third case with the cooking (*pāka*) which has become a qualifier of the agenthood denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇyartha-kartṛtva*)—if this is said, we reply: no. The construction of the agenthood denoted by the third case occurs only with an action that has not become a qualifier of an agenthood that is itself not a qualifier of something other than its own substratum (*āśraya*). Thus, the objection does not hold.

Since the aforementioned defects do not arise by accepting this etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), in cases such as *caitreṇa pācayati* ("He causes Caitra to cook"), the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is the operation that brings about the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*). In that context, since agency is a qualifier of the operation distinct from its locus, there is no obstacle to the agency expressed by the third case (*tṛtīyā*) functioning as a qualifier of the action that has acquired that qualification. Furthermore, expressions such as *caitreṇa pacati maitraḥ* ("Maitra cooks by means of Caitra") are not valid usages.

In that case, since it is impossible to convey the agency (kartṛtva) denoted by the third case-ending with respect to the action that has become a qualifier of the substratum (āśraya) by virtue of being a qualifier of the effort (kṛti), one must—intending a cognition where the effort is the qualificandum (viśeṣya)—discard the status of being a qualifier of the substratum and instead include the status of being a qualifier distinct from that [substratum], in order to exclude such expressions as "caitreṇa pacati" (Caitra cooks). Thus [it is concluded].

"But for those who have composed the *Jñānaratnaprakāśikā*, the meaning of [rules] such as 'the third case-ending occurs when the agent is not already expressed' (*anabhihite kartari tṛtīyā*) is as follows: the third case-ending and so forth occur after that which is co-occurrent with itself (the word) and is general, provided that it lacks the intentionality of denoting an agency defined by any action whatsoever co-occurrent with itself, which resides in the meaning that constitutes its own primary intended object."

Nor should it be argued that there would be the undesirable consequence of a third case ending after the word *caitra* in sentences such as "Caitra eats cooked food" (*pakvāni bhuṅkte caitraḥ*), because the absence of the intentionality (*tātparya*) whose object is the agency residing in Caitra (regarding the act of cooking, etc. exists in all words co-occurring with [the verb]. This is not to be said.

There is no inconsistency in taking as a qualifier of the referent of the term *sva* (itself) the property of being distinct from that which causes the objective relation directed toward the objective relation residing in the agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, as determined by the primary action expressed by the word uttered in co-utterance with *sva*; for in examples such as "Caitra eats what has been cooked," the term *ātman* possesses the property of being distinct from words such as "I" (*aham*), which cause the objective relation directed toward the objective relation residing in the agency expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in the primary action.

They say that because the absence of the intention to express the agency of entering—which resides in the object intended as the primary referent of the word *ātman*—is present in all words co-occurring with it, the use of the third case ending after the word *ātman* is justified.

In this regard, although in sentences such as "Maitra sees the jar being seen by Caitra," there is an impossibility of using the accusative case because the word *ghaṭa* lacks the property of being distinct from that which serves as the instigator of the objective state (*viṣayatā*)—the latter being subsumed under the objective state expressed by the primary action denoted by the suffix *śānac*.

Nor should it be argued that there is no inconsistency in our system (siddhānta) because the objectness (*viṣayatā*), which consists in conjunction with cognition, is differentiated by the differentiation of cognitions; for in our system, since cognition is a substance (*dravya*) and possesses the quality of expansion (*prasaraṇavat*), objectness is simply the conjunction with that [cognition]. Even so, in the case of a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*)—which, being connected to a jar, is a stable substance—if that cognition is a single entity, then in such a situation, with the intent of [the cognition] grasping what has already been grasped, the linguistic usage "he knows what is already known" would be untenable.

In this regard, since there is unity between the primary and secondary actions, their conjunction is also unified; thus, by means of the *kta* suffix, only the status of being the object (*karman*) of the primary action is expressed. Nevertheless, their intention is that in the case of a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*), there is merely an uninterrupted succession of cognitions, and not a single, unitary cognition.

And if—in the case of a continuous stream of cognition (dhārāvāhikajñāna)—the identity of the cognitions is both an empirical fact and established by our own philosophical tenets, then there is no inconsistency even in that instance according to the method we have stated. Thus, it is established that the differentiation of names and forms preceded by entry [into the world] belongs to the Supreme Self alone.

"But is this not untenable?"—because the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the Supreme Self is accepted. For "entry" (*anupraveśa*) consists of a specific kind of motion characterized by internal conjunction. And such motion has been pointed out by the Author of the Sūtras himself as a proof for the absence of all-pervasiveness, in the words: "Because of departure, going, and returning. Therefore, it is logical that entry belongs only to the atomic individual soul (*jīva*). If this is argued, it is replied: even though entry takes the form of a specific kind of motion, it resides in the individual soul.

There is no inconsistency, because [the world] is produced by the action of the Supreme Self and thus has Him as its agent. For instance, according to the system of the Naiyāyikas and others, in the statement "Devadatta goes to the village," even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is all-pervading (*vibhu*), what is perceived in the self as delimited by Devadatta’s body is simply the possession of an effort conducive to that bodily action which is favorable to the conjunction [with the destination]; it is not, however, the possession of an action in the form of going itself. This is because it is accepted that in all cases, there is only the manifestation in the self of an effort conducive to an action residing in the body.

Likewise, in the passage "having entered, let me evolve name and form," since it is accepted that the meaning of the suffix *-lyap*—which denotes a time subsequent to the root-meaning of "entering"—is construed with the "evolution of name and form" through a relation of substratum qualified by having the same agent as its own base-meaning, there appears in the Supreme Self the possession of an effort conducive to entering into the body in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), but not the state of being the locus of entry itself; thus, there is no inconsistency.

Nor should it be argued that even if the individual soul (*jīva*) were all-pervading (*vibhu*), its agency regarding movement and so forth would still be possible, because agency toward actions such as going, which reside in the body, can exist—just as in the case of "he goes to the village. This is because the Sūtra concerning departure (*utkrānti*) and so forth is intended to refute the Nyāya position. To explain: with the inference—"the *jīva* lacks all-pervasiveness, because it possesses action"—in mind, the Sūtra beginning with "departure" (*utkrānti*) was composed to dispel the suspicion of the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the reason (*svarūpāsiddhi*).

And thus—the point is that because [the reason] is established by scripture through such means as "departure" (utkrānti), there is no lack of essential nature (svarūpāsiddhi). Furthermore, its status as a logical reason cannot be based on a nature such as "being an action delimited by conjunction with an upward location," because—unlike the case of fire and smoke—that would be redundant (vaiyarthyāt).

Now, by the scriptural passage establishing departure—“Then, by that light, this self departs, either through the eye, or through the head, or through other parts of the body”—and by the scriptural passages establishing going and returning—“Whosoever depart from this world, they all go to the moon; from that world they return again to this world for the sake of action”—it follows that even though the self is conscious, [the action] consists solely of the volition (kṛti) conducive to the activity of departure and so forth, which resides in the body.

"If it is argued that there is a lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*) because activity (*kriyāvattva*) is not perceived [in the self], we say no. For according to the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others, at the time of departure and so forth, since the body is absent, the cognition of the self as the locus of action—expressed by such statements as 'it departs'—is necessarily required, just as in the case of 'the chariot goes. Thus, the reason consisting of the possession of activity is indeed established in the self; this is the intended meaning of the Sūtra. This has been analyzed more extensively elsewhere."
May this exposition of the meaning of the debate, composed by Anantārya— who dwells on the Yādava mountain and is a jewel among the remaining noble lineages— flourish.
Thus,
in the works of the illustrious Anantāryavarya, who is a pearl of the lineage of Śeṣārya and a resident of the sacred Yādavādri mountain.
The Discourse on the Body is completed.
